## Proof

Let $M$ be a topological manifold (Hausdorff, second-countable, locally Euclidean of dimension $n$). Recall the relevant definitions.

**Charts and atlases.** A *chart* on $M$ is a pair $(U,\varphi)$ where $U\subseteq M$ is open and $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a homeomorphism onto an open subset. An *atlas* $\mathcal{A}=\{(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\}_{\alpha\in A}$ is a collection of charts whose domains cover $M$.

**Transition maps.** For two charts $(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha),(U_\beta,\varphi_\beta)$ with $U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\neq\varnothing$, the *transition map* (overlap map) is
$$\tau_{\beta\alpha}:=\varphi_\beta\circ\varphi_\alpha^{-1}:\varphi_\alpha(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta)\longrightarrow\varphi_\beta(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta),$$
a homeomorphism between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

**$C^r$ atlas ($r\in\{k,\infty,\omega\}$).** The atlas $\mathcal{A}$ is of class $C^r$ if every transition map $\tau_{\beta\alpha}$ is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism (i.e. $C^r$ with $C^r$ inverse). A *$C^r$ manifold* is a topological manifold together with a maximal $C^r$ atlas.

---

### The statement to prove

If $\mathcal{A}$ is a $C^r$ atlas on $M$, then the maximal atlas $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ generated by $\mathcal{A}$ is itself a $C^r$ atlas: every pair of overlapping charts in $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ has a $C^r$ transition map. This is what it means for the $C^r$ structure to be *well-defined* and for a $C^r$ manifold to "have an atlas whose overlapping [maps] are of class $C^r$."

---

### Construction of the maximal atlas

Define
$$\overline{\mathcal{A}}:=\bigl\{(V,\psi)\text{ chart on }M : (V,\psi)\text{ is }C^r\text{-compatible with every }(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\in\mathcal{A}\bigr\},$$
where "$C^r$-compatible" means: for every $\alpha$ with $V\cap U_\alpha\neq\varnothing$, the map
$$\varphi_\alpha\circ\psi^{-1}:\psi(V\cap U_\alpha)\to\varphi_\alpha(V\cap U_\alpha)$$
is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism. Clearly $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ (each chart is compatible with the $C^r$ atlas it belongs to, since the transition maps $\tau_{\beta\alpha}$ are $C^r$ by hypothesis and inverses are $C^r$ as well). So $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ covers $M$.

---

### Key lemma: pairwise compatibility in $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$

**Claim.** Any two charts $(V,\psi),(W,\chi)\in\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ are $C^r$-compatible, i.e.
$$\chi\circ\psi^{-1}:\psi(V\cap W)\longrightarrow\chi(V\cap W)$$
is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism.

**Proof.** It suffices to show $\chi\circ\psi^{-1}$ is $C^r$ (the same argument with $\psi,\chi$ swapped gives that the inverse $\psi\circ\chi^{-1}$ is $C^r$).

Let $p\in V\cap W$. Since $\mathcal{A}$ covers $M$, choose $\alpha$ with $p\in U_\alpha$. On the open neighborhood $\psi(V\cap W\cap U_\alpha)$ of $\psi(p)$ we may factor
$$\chi\circ\psi^{-1}=\underbrace{\bigl(\chi\circ\varphi_\alpha^{-1}\bigr)}_{(\star)}\circ\underbrace{\bigl(\varphi_\alpha\circ\psi^{-1}\bigr)}_{(\star\star)}.$$

- $(\star\star)=\varphi_\alpha\circ\psi^{-1}$ is $C^r$ because $(V,\psi)\in\overline{\mathcal{A}}$, hence $C^r$-compatible with $(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)$.
- $(\star)=\chi\circ\varphi_\alpha^{-1}$ is $C^r$ because $(W,\chi)\in\overline{\mathcal{A}}$, hence $C^r$-compatible with $(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)$.

By the **chain rule** (valid for $C^k$, $C^\infty$, and $C^\omega$ — see below), the composition of two $C^r$ maps is $C^r$. Therefore $\chi\circ\psi^{-1}$ is $C^r$ on $\psi(V\cap W\cap U_\alpha)$.

Now vary $p$ over all of $V\cap W$. The corresponding open sets $\{\psi(V\cap W\cap U_\alpha)\}_{\alpha}$ form an open cover of $\psi(V\cap W)$. Since $\chi\circ\psi^{-1}$ is $C^r$ on each member of an open cover, it is $C^r$ on all of $\psi(V\cap W)$. $\square$

---

### Why the chain rule applies in all three classes

- **$C^k$ ($1\le k<\infty$):** the classical chain rule gives $D(g\circ f)=Dg\cdot Df$; if $f,g$ are $C^k$ then $Df,Dg$ are $C^{k-1}$, so $D(g\circ f)$ is $C^{k-1}$, hence $g\circ f$ is $C^k$.
- **$C^\infty$:** smooth maps are closed under composition, since the chain rule holds at every order of differentiation.
- **$C^\omega$ (real-analytic):** if $f$ is analytic near $x_0$ and $g$ is analytic near $f(x_0)$, then $g\circ f$ admits a convergent power-series expansion near $x_0$ (substitution of the power series of $f$ into that of $g$ yields a convergent series). Hence the composition is analytic.

In every case the inverse of a $C^r$ diffeomorphism is $C^r$ (inverse function theorem, which holds in all three classes), so the transition maps are genuine $C^r$ diffeomorphisms.

---

### Conclusion

Starting from any $C^r$ atlas $\mathcal{A}$, the maximal atlas $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ it generates is a $C^r$ atlas: by the lemma, every pair of overlapping charts in $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ has a $C^r$ transition map. Thus a $C^k$ (resp. $C^\infty$, $C^\omega$) manifold — defined as a manifold carrying a maximal $C^r$ atlas — genuinely possesses an atlas whose overlap maps are all of class $C^k$ (resp. $C^\infty$, $C^\omega$). The argument relies only on (i) the covering property of the original atlas and (ii) closure of the class $C^r$ under composition and inversion, which is exactly what the chain rule and inverse function theorem provide in each of the three regularity classes.
